In addition, new approaches have been developed to separate astrophysical effects from early galaxies from fundamental-physics effects on small-scale structure. With the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the 21~cm forest will therefore provide a promising route to study early heating, possible exotic energy injection, dark matter properties, neutrino mass, the running spectral index, and baryon--dark-matter relative velocity. This chapter reviews recent developments in 21~cm forest research and discusses observational strategies and prospects for constraining the first galaxies and fundamental physics with SKA-Low.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews advances in detecting and analyzing 21 cm forest absorption features from neutral hydrogen during reionization, highlighting new methods and the potential of SKA-Low to probe early Universe physics and structure formation.
AI.motivation: To utilize the 21 cm forest absorption features as a probe of the neutral intergalactic medium during the epoch of reionization, and to overcome challenges in detection to constrain the early Universe's thermal history and small-scale structure physics.
AI.method: Development of new statistical observables to enhance sensitivity, updated radio-source counts for better background quasar estimates, application of deep-learning techniques for efficient extraction of physical information, and innovative approaches to separate astrophysical effects from fundamental physics influences.
AI.result: The 21 cm forest, especially with the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), is established as a promising tool to study early Universe phenomena such as early heating, exotic energy injections, dark matter properties, neutrino mass, running spectral index, and baryon-dark-matter velocity effects, with improved detection strategies and observational prospects.
AI.conclusion: Recent advances in observation methods and data analysis have made the 21 cm forest a viable and powerful probe for constraining the properties of the first galaxies and fundamental physics during the epoch of reionization using instruments like SKA-Low.

title: Euclid preparation. First investigation of the impact of cross-contamination on spectroscopic redshift measurements with pixel-level simulations
summary: We present a study on simulated data focused on understanding the performance of the spectroscopic redshift measurements with the Near-Infrared Spectrometer and Photometer (NISP) instrument on Euclid. Simulations include scenarios with different levels of cross-contamination arising from overlapping spectra of nearby sources, which represents one of the main drawbacks of slitless spectroscopy. We present a new analysis based on pixel-level simulations of the NISP images, with the data processed using the Euclid spectroscopic pipeline. We first consider an idealised case with non-overlapping spectra to assess the accuracy and reliability of the redshift measurement as a function of the flux of the H-alpha emission line and galaxy size. We then introduce more realistic contamination scenarios, distinguishing between two contributions: contamination from H-alpha emitters, which are the Euclid targets for cosmological analyses, and contamination from all other galaxies. In the second case, we analyse the impact of cross-contamination with an increasing number of contaminants, from the brighter to the fainter galaxies. Given that our results show no clear evidence that sources fainter than magnitude 20 degrade redshift measurements, we conservatively restrict our analysis to galaxies with magnitudes up to 24. In particular, we provide a preliminary estimate that contamination from galaxies within the same redshift range as the target sample contributes to about 4% of the total degradation due to cross-contamination from all galaxies.

AI.tldr: This study uses pixel-level simulations to assess how overlapping spectra affect Euclid NISP's redshift measurements, finding minor impact from contaminating sources within the target redshift range and negligible degradation from faint galaxies beyond magnitude 20.
AI.motivation: To understand and quantify the impact of cross-contamination on spectroscopic redshift measurements using the NISP instrument on Euclid, addressing challenges inherent to slitless spectroscopy.
AI.method: Performed pixel-level simulations of NISP images under various contamination scenarios, processed through the Euclid spectroscopic pipeline; analyzed redshift measurement accuracy for idealized non-overlapping spectra and progressively more contaminated spectra from H-alpha emitters and other galaxies.
AI.result: Found that contamination from galaxies within the same redshift range contributes roughly 4% to total redshift measurement degradation due to cross-contamination; determined that sources fainter than magnitude 20 do not significantly degrade measurements, restricting analysis to galaxies up to magnitude 24.
AI.conclusion: Cross-contamination effects on spectroscopic redshift measurements in Euclid can be quantitatively constrained, with contamination from targets within the same redshift range being a minor contributor to overall degradation, supporting effective redshift measurement strategies in slitless spectroscopy.

title: Imaging the 21-cm Signal from the Cosmic Dawn & Epoch of Reionization and the Connection with the Global Signal
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Bag01
summary: The original baseline design for SKA-Low was motivated by the ability to produce tomographic images of the redshifted 21-cm signal, thus allowing the research field to move beyond the simple statistic of the power spectrum. In this chapter we review the imaging capabilities of SKA-Low, the wide variety of methods proposed for quantatively analysing image data, as well as the connection with the global 21-cm signal.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews SKA-Low's imaging abilities and methods to analyze 21-cm signal data, aimed at enhancing cosmological insights through tomographic imaging.
AI.motivation: To enable tomographic imaging of the redshifted 21-cm signal for advancing research beyond power spectrum statistics.
AI.method: Review of SKA-Low's imaging capabilities and various quantitative analysis methods for image data, and exploration of the connection with the global 21-cm signal.
AI.result: An overview of the SKA-Low imaging performance and diverse analytical approaches, highlighting their relevance to 21-cm cosmology.
AI.conclusion: SKA-Low's design facilitates detailed tomographic studies of the redshifted 21-cm signal, broadening the scope of cosmological investigations beyond power spectrum analysis.

title: Interferometric HI Intensity Mapping of the Late Time Universe with SKA-Mid
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Mazumder01
summary: We discuss the progress towards using the SKA-Mid for interferometric neutral hydrogen (HI) intensity mapping surveys. By mapping the distribution of cosmic HI distribution through the 21cm line, SKA-Mid will be able to measure the HI power spectrum at small angular separations in interferometric mode. We review the measurements made from the precursor MeerKAT telescope, using the MeerKAT DEEP2 as well as the MIGHTEE survey data, yielding tentative detection as well as upper limits on HI clustering. The methodology for MeerKAT can be naturally extended to SKA-Mid. Forecasts suggest that SKA-Mid AA4 will be able to measure the HI power spectrum with high statistical significance across a wide range of redshifts from $z\sim1.0$ to $z\sim 3.0$, around nonlinear scales $k\sim 1.0\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. The precise measurements can be used to constrain the properties of HI galaxies, providing a novel window into probing galaxy evolution at $1.0\lesssim z \lesssim 3.0$.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews progress in HI intensity mapping with SKA-Mid, using MeerKAT data as precursor results, and forecasts that SKA-Mid will precisely measure the HI power spectrum from redshift 1 to 3, advancing galaxy evolution studies.
AI.motivation: To leverage the capabilities of SKA-Mid for interferometric HI intensity mapping to probe cosmic HI distribution and galaxy evolution.
AI.method: Using interferometric measurements of the 21cm HI line to map the HI power spectrum; extending methodologies developed from MeerKAT precursor observations (DEEP2 and MIGHTEE survey) to SKA-Mid.
AI.result: Tentative HI clustering detections and upper limits from MeerKAT; forecasts indicate SKA-Mid AA4 can achieve high-significance HI power spectrum measurements from redshift 1 to 3 around nonlinear scales.
AI.conclusion: SKA-Mid will enable precise measurements of HI clustering, improving constraints on HI galaxy properties and offering new insights into galaxy evolution at redshifts 1 to 3.

title: Using SKAO to Understand the Clustering of Gravitational Wave Sources
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Bosi01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Coalescing Binary Black Holes (BBHs) trace the Large-Scale Structure (LSS) of the Universe, and their clustering properties can be extracted from Gravitational Wave (GW) data. Next-generation detectors, such as the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer, will enable statistical studies of GW sources thanks to the massive number of detected events. However, such events will still suffer from significant instrumental and theoretical uncertainties. Cross-correlating GW maps with other LSS surveys provides a promising strategy to mitigate these limitations. The SKA-Mid intensity mapping and radio continuum surveys offer ideal datasets for cross-correlation studies with GWs (SKAO$\times$ET2CE). Their wide sky coverage and deep redshift sensitivity will allow precise probing of the epochs and environments where stellar BBHs form most efficiently. In this chapter, we forecast the potential of cross-correlation angular power spectra to extract information on the distribution and clustering properties of GW events. First, we model the number density and bias of three independent tracers: GW sources, neutral hydrogen intensity maps, and radio galaxies. We estimate the constraining power of SKA-Mid$\times$ET2CE on the GW clustering bias, which carries information on the origin of GW progenitors, e.g., whether they formed through stellar evolution or are primordial black holes. Finally, we develop a semi-analytic model for GW events hosted by SKAO galaxies as a function of the time-delay distribution between the binary formation and merger, which is still largely uncertain to date. We forecast the signal-to-noise ratio of their cross-correlation with SKA-Mid, and demonstrate that SKA-Mid$\times$ET2CE will foster our understanding of the time-delay distribution.

AI.tldr: This study forecasts that cross-correlating gravitational wave data from future detectors with SKA-Mid radio surveys will significantly improve insights into binary black hole formation and clustering, helping to distinguish their origins and understand merger time delays.
AI.motivation: Next-generation GW detectors will detect many events but with significant uncertainties; cross-correlation with other large-scale structure surveys can mitigate these limitations and improve understanding of BBH distributions and origins.
AI.method: Modeling number density and bias of GW sources, neutral hydrogen intensity maps, and radio galaxies; forecasting cross-correlation angular power spectra between GW maps and SKA-Mid datasets; developing a semi-analytic model for GW events including time-delay distributions; estimating signal-to-noise ratios for cross-correlation analysis.
AI.result: SKA-Mid×ET2CE cross-correlation will enable precise probing of BBH formation environments, constrain GW clustering bias informing on progenitor origins, and improve understanding of the time-delay distribution between BBH formation and merger.
AI.conclusion: Cross-correlation of GW data from next-generation detectors with SKA-Mid LSS surveys is a promising strategy to overcome GW detection uncertainties and extract key astrophysical information on BBH clustering, formation channels, and merger time delays.

title: The 3D clustering of Lyman Alpha Emitters measured with DESI
summary: We present a clustering analysis of Lyman-$α$ emitters (LAEs) using spectroscopic observations from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) of candidates selected from the Blanco/DECam Intermediate-Band Imaging Survey (IBIS). We measure the two-point correlation function and the power spectrum, including cross-correlations with DESI quasars. Using both analytical and halo occupation distribution (HOD) simulation-based modeling, we find a linear bias of $b \sim 2.31$--$2.62$ for LAEs over the redshift range $2.26 < z < 3.41$. The analytical modeling also provides constraints on the strength of radiative transfer effects, while the HOD analysis characterizes the LAE-halo connection across multiple models. Finally, we quantify the magnitude of non-perturbative clustering effects such as Fingers of God in the LAE population, providing essential input for the accurate modeling of LAE-based cosmological analyses in forthcoming high-redshift surveys such as DESI-II.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes clustering of LAEs using DESI spectroscopic data, finding their bias, constraining radiative transfer effects, modeling halo connections, and quantifying small-scale clustering distortions, aiding future high-redshift cosmological studies.
AI.motivation: To understand the clustering properties and halo connection of Lyman-alpha emitters (LAEs) using spectroscopic data, enabling accurate cosmological analyses in future high-redshift surveys.
AI.method: Spectroscopic observations of LAE candidates from DESI and IBIS were analyzed by measuring the two-point correlation function and power spectrum, including cross-correlations with DESI quasars. Analytical and halo occupation distribution (HOD) simulation-based modeling were employed to interpret the data and characterize radiative transfer effects and the LAE-halo connection.
AI.result: LAEs exhibit a linear bias of approximately 2.31 to 2.62 over redshifts 2.26 to 3.41. The study constrains radiative transfer effects and describes the LAE-halo connection through multiple HOD models. Non-perturbative clustering effects, such as Fingers of God, are quantified, enhancing modeling accuracy for future LAE-based cosmological surveys.
AI.conclusion: The combined analytical and HOD modeling successfully characterizes the clustering and halo occupation of LAEs, providing key parameters and corrections essential for precise cosmological analyses in upcoming surveys like DESI-II.

title: Exploring Gravitational Wave Signatures Due to Primordial Non-gaussianity and Large Scale Structure Using SKAO
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Ragavendra01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: This chapter explores theoretical and observational strategies to use the stochastic gravitational-wave background detectable by Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) as a probe of precision cosmology. We detail the critical phenomenon of scalar-induced gravitational waves, demonstrating their unique features and their sensitivity to primordial non-Gaussianity on scales much smaller than those probed by the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure. We investigate the phenomenology of parity violation in the early Universe through the chirality imprinted in the stochastic gravitational-wave background, demonstrating that a parity-odd primordial trispectrum can generate a detectable scale-dependent helicity. On the observational side, we point out that the standard gravitational-wave angular auto-correlation analysis is significantly limited by astrophysical shot noise. We show that cross-correlating the gravitational wave signal with independent large-scale structure tracers enhances the signal-to-noise ratio and allows us to isolate the astrophysical and cosmological components in the background. These results can be achieved only thanks to the enhanced sensitivity of SKAO, extensive sky coverage, and high angular resolution, which together make such targets observationally feasible.

AI.tldr: This work proposes using SKAO to detect the stochastic gravitational-wave background for precision cosmology, revealing small-scale primordial non-Gaussianity and parity violation signatures, and overcoming observational noise by cross-correlating with large-scale structures.
AI.motivation: To utilize the stochastic gravitational-wave background detectable by SKAO as a precision tool for cosmology, probing phenomena inaccessible by other cosmic surveys.
AI.method: The paper combines theoretical modeling of scalar-induced gravitational waves and parity violation effects with observational strategies involving angular auto-correlation and cross-correlation with large-scale structure tracers, leveraging SKAO's sensitivity and resolution.
AI.result: Identification of unique features of scalar-induced gravitational waves sensitive to small-scale primordial non-Gaussianity, detection potential of parity-odd primordial trispectrum via chirality in the background, and enhancement of signal detection by cross-correlating gravitational waves with large-scale structure to overcome astrophysical shot noise limitations.
AI.conclusion: The enhanced capabilities of SKAO enable new observational avenues to probe early Universe physics, including primordial non-Gaussianity and parity violation, through the stochastic gravitational-wave background by combining advanced theoretical insights with optimized observational techniques.

title: The Topology of the Universe
comment: Invited Review for Nature Astronomy, 14 pages, 4 figures
summary: Is the Universe infinite in all directions? The only way to know is to look. A non-trivial cosmic topology would imprint subtle signatures on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and on the three-dimensional distribution of matter, breaking statistical isotropy and, potentially, homogeneity at the largest scales. If the topology scale is small enough, these signatures would be observable. Over the past three decades, successive space missions, most notably WMAP and $\textit{Planck}$, have enabled sophisticated searches for these signatures, using methods ranging from looking for matched circle pairs to full Bayesian likelihood analysis based on topology-dependent covariance matrices. Although these searches have yielded no definitive evidence for non-trivial topology, current constraints exclude only some topologies, parameter ranges, and observer positions. Recent advances show that detectable signals may persist even when the topology scale exceeds the size of the visible Universe. Planned CMB experiments, including LiteBIRD and $\textit{Taurus}$, and high-precision galaxy and line intensity-mapping surveys, could expand the detectable parameter space by exploiting polarisation data, and by exploring topology-induced correlations at all accessible redshifts. Whether cosmic topology is observable remains uncertain, but current and future data offer an unprecedented opportunity to probe the global structure of the Universe.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews efforts to detect non-trivial cosmic topology through CMB and matter distribution studies. So far, no conclusive evidence exists, but future missions could improve detection prospects by utilizing polarization and multi-redshift data.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the Universe has a non-trivial cosmic topology, which would affect the global structure and observable properties at the largest scales.
AI.method: Utilizing cosmic microwave background data and three-dimensional matter distributions from past space missions like WMAP and Planck; employing techniques such as matched circle searches and Bayesian likelihood analyses with topology-dependent covariance matrices; and planning future observations with enhanced polarization data and multi-redshift surveys.
AI.result: No definitive evidence for non-trivial topology has been found so far, but current constraints exclude only certain topologies, parameter ranges, and observer positions. Detectable signals may still exist even beyond the visible Universe scale.
AI.conclusion: While cosmic topology remains an open question, ongoing and upcoming high-precision experiments provide a promising avenue to probe the Universe's global structure beyond current observational limits.
